content.title: What are Access Modifiers and Packages?
content.description: Access modifiers control the visibility of classes, methods, and variables, while packages organize related Java classes and interfaces into namespaces for better code management.

content.content: As Java applications become larger, it becomes important to organize code and control who can access different parts of the program. Access modifiers provide security by restricting access, while packages help organize related classes and avoid naming conflicts.

content.title: Why Learn Access Modifiers?
content.content: Access modifiers improve encapsulation and security, while packages make large projects easier to organize and maintain.
Access Modifiers
Access modifiers define the visibility of classes, methods, constructors, and variables. Java provides four access levels: public, protected, default, and private.

content.title: Four Access Levels
content.description: Java provides public, protected, default (package-private), and private access modifiers to control member visibility.

content.content: public Access Modifier
The public modifier provides the highest level of accessibility. Public members can be accessed from any class in any package.

content.title: Public Example

content.content: private Access Modifier
The private modifier restricts access to the same class only. It is commonly used to achieve encapsulation.

content.title: Encapsulation
content.content: Private variables are usually accessed through public getter and setter methods.
protected Access Modifier
The protected modifier allows access within the same package and by subclasses in different packages.

content.title: Protected Example

content.content: Default Access Modifier
If no access modifier is specified, Java assigns default (package-private) access. Members are accessible only within the same package.
Introduction to Packages
A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces together. Packages improve project organization and prevent class name conflicts.
Import Statement
The import keyword allows classes from other packages to be used without writing their fully qualified names.

content.title: Import Example
content.code:
import java.util.Scanner;

Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

content.content: Built-in Packages
Java provides many predefined packages that contain commonly used classes and interfaces.
User-Defined Packages
Developers can create custom packages to organize project modules. A package name usually follows the reverse domain naming convention.
Real-Life Analogy

content.title: Office Building
content.content: Think of a company office. Different rooms have different access levels—some are open to everyone (public), some only to employees (protected), some only within a department (default), and some only to the manager (private). Packages are like departments that organize employees based on their work.

content.title: Interview Importance
content.content: Interviewers commonly ask about the differences between public, private, protected, and default access modifiers, package creation, import statements, and encapsulation.
Common Mistakes

items.question: Can a private variable be accessed directly outside its class?
items.answer: No. It must be accessed through public methods such as getters and setters.

items.question: What happens if an import statement is missing?
items.answer: The compiler cannot recognize classes from external packages unless their fully qualified names are used.

items.question: Why should meaningful package names be used?
items.answer: They improve project organization and reduce naming conflicts.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: Use private for data hiding, public for global access, protected for inheritance, default for package-level access, and packages to organize related classes.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: private provides the highest level of data protection.
Packages organize related classes and interfaces.
The import keyword allows classes from other packages to be used.
